bibl.title: Diode probes for spatiotemporal optical control of multiple neurons in freely moving animals

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: an instrument: independent optical control of many sites in the brain of a freely moving animal, with the stimulated neurons recorded at the same time
span.quote: Neuronal control with high temporal precision is possible with optogenetics, yet currently available methods do not enable to control independently multiple locations in the brains of freely moving animals. Here, we describe a diode-probe system that allows real-time and location-specific control of neuronal activity at multiple sites.

span.label: how to stimulate exactly the neurons being monitored, when electrodes hear only 60 μm and every existing light source reaches far further than that
span.quote: Since such electrodes can only record and disambiguate spikes of nearby (up to 60 μm) neurons ( Buzsáki 2004 ), stimulation of continuously monitored cells requires placing the light source very close to the recording site. However, stimulation through light sources placed on the surface of the brain ( Huber et al. 2008 ) or large fibers placed in the brain parenchyma a few hundred micrometers from the recording sites ( Airan et al. 2009 ; Anikeeva et al. 2011 ; Cardin et al. 2010 ; Halassa et al. 2011 ; Han et al. 2009 ; Kravitz et al. 2010 ) inevitably activates many more unmonitored neurons than are being monitored, making the separation between direct and population-mediated effects impossible. Moreover, the high intensity used for the activation of deep neurons may generate superposition of multiple spike waveforms ( Royer et al. 2010 ) and considerable light artifacts ( Cardin et al. 2010 ; Han et al. 2009 ; Kravitz et al. 2010 ).

span.label: a diode-fiber assembly light enough to put one on every shank - local photostimulation and recording of the same cells, without light artifacts, spike superposition or a fiber tether
span.quote: Neuronal control with high temporal precision is possible with optogenetics, yet currently available methods do not enable to control independently multiple locations in the brains of freely moving animals. Here, we describe a diode-probe system that allows real-time and location-specific control of neuronal activity at multiple sites.

span.label: method
span.quote: Here, we describe a diode-probe system that allows real-time and location-specific control of neuronal activity at multiple sites.

span.label: multisite optogenetic control of neurons in freely moving animals
span.quote: Neuronal control with high temporal precision is possible with optogenetics, yet currently available methods do not enable to control independently multiple locations in the brains of freely moving animals.

span.label: system-or-tool-building
span.quote: Here, we describe how an array of lightweight diodes is coupled to optical fibers.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Putting the fiber tip within tens of μm of the recording sites means very little light is needed, which in turn removes the need for high currents and lets the device avoid heat sinks, optical artifacts and spike superposition while confining the effect to the monitored neurons
span.quote: This enables driving small diodes with low currents, avoiding bulky heat sinks and collimating optics, preventing optical artifacts and spike superposition, and limiting the spatial extent of the photostimulus effect to a relatively small number of neurons, which are concurrently monitored by the extracellular electrodes.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: An index-matched glue at the diode–fiber interface cuts Fresnel reflection losses and widens the fiber's acceptance angle for skew rays, which is why coupled power doubles
span.quote: Since the refractive index (RI) of the glue is higher than air (1.56–1.57), the drop of glue reduced Fresnel losses and approximately doubled the acceptance angle of the fiber to skew rays

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Red-light-driven halorhodopsin hyperpolarisation of the membrane delays the ChR2-evoked spike, which is why latencies lengthen when activation and silencing are applied together
span.quote: albeit with a longer latency supposedly due to the red light-induced hyperpolarization of the membrane

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The unusually high fraction of responsive units follows from the high AAV transduction rate combined with the very short distance between fiber tip and recording sites
span.quote: This relatively high fraction of light-modulated units may be due to the high ChR2 transduction rates typically obtained with AAV vehicles

span.label: the light is weak and the fiber tip is close, so the illuminated volume is about 0.001 mm 3 - the cells the light reaches are the cells the shank can hear
span.quote: The volume of the illuminated brain tissue [at an intensity of >1 mW/mm 2 , the documented threshold for stimulating channelrhodopsin2 (ChR2); Aravanis et al. 2007 ; Boyden et al. 2005 ] was ∼0.001 mm 3 , formed by a truncated cone with 180-μm height and 150-μm base diameter ( Figs. 1 B and 3 ). Red laser diodes driven by similar currents yielded ∼180 μW at the fiber tip and subtended a similar volume [at an intensity of >7 mW/mm 2 , a level sufficient for stimulating halorhodopsin eNpHR3.0 (Halo) with red light; Gradinaru et al. 2010 ]. Assuming neuronal density of 20,000–100,000 cells/mm 3 ( Braitenberg and Schüz 1998 ; West et al. 1991 ), the illuminated volume contained an estimated number of 20–100 cells, many of which can be monitored by a multisite shank of a silicon probe ( Buzsáki 2004 ). The number of illuminated neurons, which is in direct proportion to light intensity at the fiber tip ( Fig. 3 B , bottom left ), could be controlled by varying the diode current.

span.label: a drop of index-matching glue at the diode-fiber interface, which cuts the reflective losses at each interface from 8% to under 1%
span.quote: Using a coupling interface with an index similar to the indices of the source and fiber ( n in ≈ n source ≈ n core ; e.g., NOA-61, Norland Products; RI of 1.56/1.57 for red/blue light) reduces these reflective losses considerably (to <1%) but at a cost of reducing the effective acceptance angle γ of the fiber by a factor of (1/1.57) 2 = 41%.

span.label: and the same glue admits skew rays from all directions, which is where the doubling in coupling efficiency actually comes from
span.quote: θ Is typically much larger than γ (for the above fiber, the values are 12.7 and 43.6°), and thus a considerable part of noncollimated light accepted into a multimode fiber is from nonmeridional rays ( Colvin 1974 ). Although not all rays falling within the θ cone will be transmitted (the exact fraction exhibits a complex dependency on γ, n 0 , and the angle of the ray relative to the fiber axis; Potter 1961 ), the effect of applying an index-matching medium on the skew rays acceptance angle θ is diametrically opposite from that on acceptance angle of meridional rays, γ. For instance, applying a coupling medium with an index higher than the core index (e.g., 1.57) enables acceptance of skew rays from all directions, yielding a twofold increase in the coupling efficiency (see below).

span.label: with the light path perpendicular to the recording sites and the power several orders of magnitude below laser stimulation, so there are no local field potential artifacts to interpret
span.quote: The weak (<40 μW) light stimulus did not result in local field potential (LFP) artifacts ( Figs. 5 B , 6 A , 7 A , and 8 A ) as often seen when light power several orders of magnitude higher is used (1–10 mW; Cardin et al. 2010 ; Han et al. 2009 ; Kravitz et al. 2010 ).

span.label: The spatial confinement of the photostimulus is itself a drawback for experiments that need a whole structure controlled synchronously.
span.note: what this limits: the confinement that is the method's selling point: FOR SOME APPLICATIONS, THE USE OF SPATIALLY RESTRICTED PHOTOSTIMULATION FOR LOCALIZED NEURONAL CONTROL IS ACTUALLY A LIMITATION - an advantage for one use and a defect for another
span.quote: For some applications, the use of spatially restricted photostimulation for localized neuronal control is actually a limitation.

span.label: The 1/d scattering model used to estimate light intensity overestimates power beyond 1 mm from the fiber tip.
span.note: what this limits: every light-intensity figure beyond 1 mm from the tip: THE MODEL CONSISTENTLY OVERESTIMATED POWER AT DISTANCES >1 MM, while POWER AT SHORTER DISTANCES WAS WELL-APPROXIMATED
span.quote: Although the model consistently overestimated power at distances >1 mm, power at shorter distances was well-approximated ( r 2 > 0.98 in all cases).

span.label: The fluorescein-bath measurement of the light cone is only an approximation of the real geometric light distribution in brain tissue.
span.note: what this limits: the measured light cone: THIS IS ONLY A PROXY TO THE REAL GEOMETRIC DISTRIBUTION OF LIGHT IN THE BRAIN SINCE SCATTERING MAY CONTRIBUTE ... ESPECIALLY AT SHORT WAVELENGTHS
span.quote: note that this is only a proxy to the real geometric distribution of light in the brain since scattering may contribute to the geometric distribution, especially at short wavelengths

span.label: THE PAPER'S HEADLINE ADVANTAGE, RE-TAGGED AS A LIMITATION: spatially restricted photostimulation IS ACTUALLY A LIMITATION for experiments requiring synchronous control of an entire structure
span.note: what this limits: experiments requiring synchronous control of an entire structure, where the spatial extent should be two to three orders of magnitude higher than the 0.001 mm 3 a shank can monitor
span.quote: For some applications, the use of spatially restricted photostimulation for localized neuronal control is actually a limitation. For instance, in experiments requiring synchronous control of an entire structure, the spatial extent of light stimulation should be two to three orders of magnitude higher than the ∼0.001 mm 3 that can also be monitored electrophysiologically by a multisite shank of a silicon probe

span.label: the scattering model consistently overestimated power beyond 1 mm, and scattering ran 5 to 10% higher in tissue that was not fresh
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 1, plus the tissue caveat: SCATTERING WAS SLIGHTLY HIGHER (5-10%) IN NONFRESH TISSUE
span.quote: Although the model consistently overestimated power at distances >1 mm, power at shorter distances was well-approximated ( r 2 > 0.98 in all cases). The fit did not depend on tip morphology (cleaved or pointed), source power, or the brain region used, although scattering was slightly higher (5–10%) in nonfresh tissue.

span.label: the fluorescein image is declared A PROXY ONLY for the real geometric distribution of light in the brain, since scattering contributes to it at short wavelengths
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 2 - the fluorescein image stands in for the real distribution
span.quote: note that this is only a proxy to the real geometric distribution of light in the brain since scattering may contribute to the geometric distribution, especially at short wavelengths

span.label: the high fraction of light-modulated units MAY BE DUE TO transduction rates and the proximity of the fiber tip rather than to anything general
span.note: what this limits: the fraction of units reported as light-modulated: it MAY BE DUE TO THE HIGH ChR2 TRANSDUCTION RATES ... AND THE PROXIMITY OF THE FIBER TIP TO THE RECORDING SITES
span.quote: This relatively high fraction of light-modulated units may be due to the high ChR2 transduction rates typically obtained with AAV vehicles (40–80%; Cardin et al. 2010 ; Diester et al. 2011 ) and the proximity of the fiber tip to the recording sites (≥50 μm).

span.label: and the count of illuminated cells rests on an assumed neuronal density and IGNORES SHADOWING by the probe shank
span.note: what this limits: the count of illuminated cells: THE ESTIMATION ... ASSUMES NEURONAL DENSITY OF 20,000 CELLS/MM3 AND IGNORES SHADOWING BY THE PROBE SHANK
span.quote: The estimation, shown for 2 different intensity thresholds for ChR2 activation, assumes neuronal density of 20,000 cells/mm 3 and ignores shadowing by the probe shank.

span.label: with the number of fibers a freely moving animal can be tethered to limited to one or two, which RESTRICTED the range of scientific questions that could be addressed
span.note: what this limits: what could be asked before this method, not only what could be measured: SINCE THE NUMBER OF FIBERS A FREELY MOVING ANIMAL CAN BE TETHERED TO IS LIMITED (1-2 FOR SMALL RODENTS), THE RANGE OF SCIENTIFIC QUESTIONS THAT COULD BE ADDRESSED WAS RESTRICTED
span.quote: These issues were previously addressed in part by coupling small-core fibers to DPSS lasers driven at low power ( Royer et al. 2010 ), but since the number of fibers a freely moving animal can be tethered to is limited (1–2 for small rodents), the range of scientific questions that could be addressed was restricted.

span.label: for a uniform planar (Lambertian) light source and a straight cleaved optical fiber having a numerical aperture, the maximum coupling efficiency of Hudson 1974
span.quote: For a uniform planar (Lambertian) light source of area A s and a straight (cleaved) optical fiber of cross-sectional area A f having a numerical aperture NA in , the maximum coupling efficiency is ( Hudson 1974 )

span.label: reflective losses, quantified by the Fresnel equations at each interface, and skew rays - two factors with opposing practical implications, both ignored in the standard coupling formula
span.quote: Two factors, which have opposing practical implications, were ignored in the foregoing: 1 ) reflective losses; and 2 ) skew rays. Since there are inevitable differences between the RIs of the source, coupling medium, and fiber core, there is attenuation due to reflection at each interface. This is quantified by the Fresnel equations; for unpolarized light traveling from a source with RI of n s to a target n t , the attenuation is 1 − ( n s − n t ) 2 /( n s + n t ) 2 at each interface. For empirical RI values (e.g., diode die: 1.525; fiber core: 1.457; and air: 1), there is 8% loss due to reflections.

span.label: a 1/d scattering model fitted to power measured through a block of brain, giving a scattering coefficient per wavelength
span.quote: The mean (± SE) scattering coefficients depended on wavelength and were ( Fig. 3 A , bottom left ): blue light, 7.18 ± 0.17; orange, 4.37 ± 0.15; and red, 3.44 ± 0.05. For blue light, the current value is smaller than previously reported values (10.3 for the rat brain; Aravanis et al. 2007 ). The mismatch could be explained by the slightly different testing conditions. In previous measurements, light was shined through brain slices, which causes reflective losses and may result in a higher calculated spatial attenuation. In any event, estimates of spatial attenuation of light intensity (see below) were similar regardless of the precise number used (<10% change in the range of 6–9 for blue light; 2.5–4.5 for red light).

span.label: red laser diodes driven by similar currents, yielding light at the fiber tip that subtended a similar illuminated volume of brain tissue
span.quote: The volume of the illuminated brain tissue [at an intensity of >1 mW/mm 2 , the documented threshold for stimulating channelrhodopsin2 (ChR2); Aravanis et al. 2007 ; Boyden et al. 2005 ] was ∼0.001 mm 3 , formed by a truncated cone with 180-μm height and 150-μm base diameter ( Figs. 1 B and 3 ). Red laser diodes driven by similar currents yielded ∼180 μW at the fiber tip and subtended a similar volume [at an intensity of >7 mW/mm 2 , a level sufficient for stimulating halorhodopsin eNpHR3.0 (Halo) with red light; Gradinaru et al. 2010 ]. Assuming neuronal density of 20,000–100,000 cells/mm 3 ( Braitenberg and Schüz 1998 ; West et al. 1991 ), the illuminated volume contained an estimated number of 20–100 cells, many of which can be monitored by a multisite shank of a silicon probe ( Buzsáki 2004 ). The number of illuminated neurons, which is in direct proportion to light intensity at the fiber tip ( Fig. 3 B , bottom left ), could be controlled by varying the diode current.

span.label: waveguides embedded in the probe shank, named as the route to scaling the number of sources
span.quote: Because the diode-probe arrays require only electrical connections, they can be used wirelessly ( Wentz et al. 2011 ), enabling recording and stimulation experiments with, for instance, freely moving birds and/or long-term naturalistic experiments with larger animals while permitting precise, large-scale, spatiotemporal control of neuronal activity. Finally, microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) technology can be used to integrate diode dies with optical waveguides embedded in the shanks of a silicon probe ( Zorzos et al. 2010 ), yielding yet smaller devices and scaling up the number of light sources.

span.label: closed-loop triggering - the recorded signal decides when the stimulus happens
span.quote: To demonstrate physiological closed-loop control in a freely moving animal, we used the activity of a well-isolated neuron recorded on one shank of a diode probe implanted in the CA1 pyramidal layer to trigger optical stimulation on multiple other shanks ( Fig. 7 A ). Comparison of the cross-correlation histograms during illumination ( Fig. 7 B ) and during baseline ( Fig. 7 C ) shows that this manipulation resulted in transient modification of cross-correlation patterns in the network and illustrates that diode probes can be used to study plasticity mechanisms in vivo.

span.label: spike waveforms during light compared with waveforms during spontaneous activity
span.quote: Moreover, extracellular spikes were not superimposed and distorted by the weak light pulses ( Royer et al. 2010 ), as spike waveforms during light and during spontaneous activity were similar (median waveform consistencies for light-modulated/nonresponsive units: 0.977/0.983; U test, P = 0.19; Fig. 4 D ).

span.label: units recorded on the shanks that were NOT illuminated, 200 μm and further away
span.quote: Fixing light intensity to 0.1–0.2 mW/mm 2 at the shank center, we found that whereas units recorded on the illuminated shank were often modulated (10 shanks in 3 rats; 20/39 units; 52%), the fraction of modulated units on other shanks (≥200 μm away) was at chance level (nearby shank: 5/73, 6.8%; exact binomial test, P > 0.05 for units recorded on any nonilluminated shank; Fig. 5 D ). Thus the multidiode/-electrode array configuration enables not only temporally precise, but also spatial control in a small volume of intact brain, which can be monitored simultaneously by the recording electrodes.

span.label: the same cross-correlation histograms computed over a duration-matched baseline period before any stimulation
span.quote: Note that the precise temporal correlations in B were generated by the photostimuli, as CCHs between the same units were nearly flat (with an exception of a 1-ms lag between the units recorded on shanks 4 and 3 ) before the stimulation.

span.label: the wideband traces inspected for photoelectrical artifacts at the light powers actually used
span.quote: The weak (<40 μW) light stimulus did not result in local field potential (LFP) artifacts ( Figs. 5 B , 6 A , 7 A , and 8 A ) as often seen when light power several orders of magnitude higher is used (1–10 mW; Cardin et al. 2010 ; Han et al. 2009 ; Kravitz et al. 2010 ).

span.label: the scattering fit repeated across tip morphology, source power and brain region
span.quote: Although the model consistently overestimated power at distances >1 mm, power at shorter distances was well-approximated ( r 2 > 0.98 in all cases). The fit did not depend on tip morphology (cleaved or pointed), source power, or the brain region used, although scattering was slightly higher (5–10%) in nonfresh tissue.

span.label: THE PAPER'S HEADLINE ADVANTAGE, RE-TAGGED AS A LIMITATION BY ITS OWN AUTHORS: for some applications the use of SPATIALLY RESTRICTED PHOTOSTIMULATION for localized neuronal control IS ACTUALLY A LIMITATION - where synchronous control of an entire structure is wanted, the spatial extent should be two to three ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE HIGHER than the 0.001 mm 3 that can be monitored
span.quote: For some applications, the use of spatially restricted photostimulation for localized neuronal control is actually a limitation. For instance, in experiments requiring synchronous control of an entire structure, the spatial extent of light stimulation should be two to three orders of magnitude higher than the ∼0.001 mm 3 that can also be monitored electrophysiologically by a multisite shank of a silicon probe

span.label: and the resolution is not a better setting but a different question - THE SPECIFIC LIGHT SOURCES AND FIBERS SHOULD BE TAILORED TO THE SCIENTIFIC QUESTION AT HAND
span.quote: Alternatively, if the goal is to generate activity patterns in a large volume of brain sequentially or synchronously, multiple light sources coupled to small-diameter fibers can be used ( Figs. 7 – 9 ). Thus the specific light sources and fibers should be tailored to the scientific question at hand.

span.quote: Using a coupling interface with an index similar to the indices of the source and fiber ( n in ≈ n source ≈ n core ; e.g., NOA-61, Norland Products; RI of 1.56/1.57 for red/blue light) reduces these reflective losses considerably (to <1%) but at a cost of reducing the effective acceptance angle γ of the fiber by a factor of (1/1.57) 2 = 41%.

span.label: the same glue on the other component: its effect on the SKEW RAYS acceptance angle is DIAMETRICALLY OPPOSITE from its effect on the meridional one, enabling acceptance from all directions and A TWOFOLD INCREASE in coupling efficiency - the net sign is empirical, not derivable
span.quote: θ Is typically much larger than γ (for the above fiber, the values are 12.7 and 43.6°), and thus a considerable part of noncollimated light accepted into a multimode fiber is from nonmeridional rays ( Colvin 1974 ). For instance, applying a coupling medium with an index higher than the core index (e.g., 1.57) enables acceptance of skew rays from all directions, yielding a twofold increase in the coupling efficiency (see below).

span.label: with the two ignored factors named as ignored: TWO FACTORS, WHICH HAVE OPPOSING PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS, WERE IGNORED IN THE FOREGOING - reflective losses, and skew rays
span.quote: Two factors, which have opposing practical implications, were ignored in the foregoing: 1 ) reflective losses; and 2 ) skew rays. Since there are inevitable differences between the RIs of the source, coupling medium, and fiber core, there is attenuation due to reflection at each interface. This is quantified by the Fresnel equations; for unpolarized light traveling from a source with RI of n s to a target n t , the attenuation is 1 − ( n s − n t ) 2 /( n s + n t ) 2 at each interface. For empirical RI values (e.g., diode die: 1.525; fiber core: 1.457; and air: 1), there is 8% loss due to reflections.

span.label: A MEASURED CONSTANT THAT DISAGREES WITH THE PUBLISHED ONE, AND THE DISAGREEMENT DECLARED NOT TO MATTER: blue-light scattering 7.18 against a previously reported 10.3 for rat brain, explained by the slightly different testing conditions - and IN ANY EVENT estimates were SIMILAR REGARDLESS OF THE PRECISE NUMBER USED
span.quote: The mean (± SE) scattering coefficients depended on wavelength and were ( Fig. 3 A , bottom left ): blue light, 7.18 ± 0.17; orange, 4.37 ± 0.15; and red, 3.44 ± 0.05. For blue light, the current value is smaller than previously reported values (10.3 for the rat brain; Aravanis et al. 2007 ). The mismatch could be explained by the slightly different testing conditions. In previous measurements, light was shined through brain slices, which causes reflective losses and may result in a higher calculated spatial attenuation. In any event, estimates of spatial attenuation of light intensity (see below) were similar regardless of the precise number used (<10% change in the range of 6–9 for blue light; 2.5–4.5 for red light).

span.label: the model's own failure stated with its range: it CONSISTENTLY OVERESTIMATED power beyond 1 mm while fitting well below it, and scattering was 5 to 10% higher in nonfresh tissue
span.quote: Although the model consistently overestimated power at distances >1 mm, power at shorter distances was well-approximated ( r 2 > 0.98 in all cases). The fit did not depend on tip morphology (cleaved or pointed), source power, or the brain region used, although scattering was slightly higher (5–10%) in nonfresh tissue.

span.label: and the empirical map declared a proxy: THIS IS ONLY A PROXY to the real geometric distribution of light in the brain, since scattering may contribute, ESPECIALLY AT SHORT WAVELENGTHS
span.quote: note that this is only a proxy to the real geometric distribution of light in the brain since scattering may contribute to the geometric distribution, especially at short wavelengths

span.label: WHY THE LIGHT HAS TO BE WEAK AND CLOSE: electrodes can only disambiguate spikes of neurons up to 60 μm away, so stimulating from the surface or from a fiber a few hundred μm off INEVITABLY ACTIVATES MANY MORE UNMONITORED NEURONS THAN ARE BEING MONITORED, MAKING THE SEPARATION BETWEEN DIRECT AND POPULATION-MEDIATED EFFECTS IMPOSSIBLE
span.quote: Since such electrodes can only record and disambiguate spikes of nearby (up to 60 μm) neurons ( Buzsáki 2004 ), stimulation of continuously monitored cells requires placing the light source very close to the recording site. However, stimulation through light sources placed on the surface of the brain ( Huber et al. 2008 ) or large fibers placed in the brain parenchyma a few hundred micrometers from the recording sites ( Airan et al. 2009 ; Anikeeva et al. 2011 ; Cardin et al. 2010 ; Halassa et al. 2011 ; Han et al. 2009 ; Kravitz et al. 2010 ) inevitably activates many more unmonitored neurons than are being monitored, making the separation between direct and population-mediated effects impossible. Moreover, the high intensity used for the activation of deep neurons may generate superposition of multiple spike waveforms ( Royer et al. 2010 ) and considerable light artifacts ( Cardin et al. 2010 ; Han et al. 2009 ; Kravitz et al. 2010 ).

span.label: and strong light of ANY wavelength carries energy dissipated as HEAT, which has a MIXED DE-/HYPERPOLARIZING effect - a confound that does not depend on the opsin at all
span.quote: Second, strong light of any wavelength carries considerable energy that is dissipated in the form of heat as photons are scattered and absorbed in brain tissue. Local heating has a mixed de-/hyperpolarizing effect on neuronal activity ( Shen and Schwartzkroin 1988 ; Thompson et al. 1985 ), which may confound and/or limit the effect of optogenetic manipulations. Third, high-intensity light may generate photoelectrical artifacts manifested as LFP deflections ( Cardin et al. 2010 ; Han et al. 2009 ; Kravitz et al. 2010 ) and cause synchronous activation of nearby neurons ( Royer et al. 2010 ), limiting the interpretability of induced LFP patterns and the use of spike-sorting techniques.

span.label: THE SAME LIGHT, THE OPPOSITE SIGN, DECIDED BY THE PROMOTER: identical parameters in CA1 give robust spiking of pyramidal cells in CaMKII::ChR2 mice, and in PV::ChR2 mice spiking of interneurons FOLLOWED BY SILENCING of the nearby pyramidal cells
span.quote: When placed in the CA1 region of CaMKII::ChR2 mice, blue light stimulation (50 ms, ∼0.9 mW/mm 2 at the shank center) resulted in robust spiking of putative pyramidal cells but not of interneurons ( Fig. 5 E , left ). In contrast, blue light stimulation with identical parameters in the CA1 of PV::ChR2 mice resulted in robust spiking of interneurons followed by silencing of nearby pyramidal cells ( Fig. 5 E , right ). Thus diode probes enable spatiotemporal control of specific cell types in various species.

span.label: A 25% CHANGE IN DOSE FLIPS THE OUTCOME: 70% of the 0.35 mW/mm 2 blue pulses overcame the red-light hyperpolarization but ONLY 10% of the 0.28 mW/mm 2 pulses did - the same two opsins, the same cells, and a sharp threshold between activation and silencing
span.quote: Notably, the ability of ChR2-induced depolarization to overcome the halo-induced hyperpolarization depended sharply on blue light intensity: 70% of the 0.35 mW/mm 2 blue-light pulses but only 10% of 0.28 mW/mm 2 pulses were efficient (χ 2 -test, P < 0.01). Thus diode probes enable activation and silencing of the same neurons in freely behaving animals.

span.label: a statistical definition rescued by the data's own shape: the definition of light-modulated spiking WAS STATISTICAL, but the modulation indices exhibited a BIMODAL distribution, 0.045 against 0.76
span.quote: Although the definition of light-modulated spiking was statistical, light modulation indices (difference between firing rates during photostimulation and baseline divided by the sum) exhibited a bimodal distribution (medians for nonresponsive/light-modulated units, 0.045/0.76; U test, P < 0.001; Fig. 4 B , middle ).

span.label: with the fraction itself hedged - the relatively high fraction MAY BE DUE TO high transduction rates and the proximity of the fiber tip
span.quote: This relatively high fraction of light-modulated units may be due to the high ChR2 transduction rates typically obtained with AAV vehicles (40–80%; Cardin et al. 2010 ; Diester et al. 2011 ) and the proximity of the fiber tip to the recording sites (≥50 μm).

span.label: THE UNIT IS DEFINED BY THREE NUMBERED GATES BEFORE ANY RESULT IS COMPUTED: peak-to-peak amplitude above 50 microvolts, L ratio below 0.05, and a clear refractory period - and then a fourth for the statistics, at least 100 spikes above 0.01 spikes/s
span.quote: Units were required to fulfill the following criteria: 1 ) amplitude: peak-to-peak amplitude >50 μV; 2 ) morphological isolation: L ratio ( Schmitzer-Torbert et al. 2005 ) below 0.05; and 3 ) temporal isolation: interspike-interval histogram with a clear refractory period (count in the 1st 2 ms below 0.2 of the expected count given the counts in the 1st 20 ms; Fee et al. 1996 ). A total of 535 hippocampal and 98 neocortical units conformed to these criteria. To be included in statistical analyses ( Figs. 4 – 6 ), units were required to fire at least 100 spikes at a baseline rate >0.01 spikes/s; this yielded a data set of 135/72 hippocampal units (rat/mouse) and 39 neocortical units (rat).

span.label: an idealisation declared inside a figure legend: the estimate ASSUMES neuronal density of 20,000 cells/mm 3 and IGNORES SHADOWING by the probe shank
span.quote: The estimation, shown for 2 different intensity thresholds for ChR2 activation, assumes neuronal density of 20,000 cells/mm 3 and ignores shadowing by the probe shank.

span.label: the temporal resolution stated as three numbers that mean different things - center-of-mass 12 ms, latency 5.5 ms, and precision, the across-trial SD, 2 ms
span.quote: The temporal relations between light stimulation and spiking were quantified by two correlated measures: spiking center-of-mass (median, 12 ms; n = 57 light-modulated units; Fig. 5 A , left ) and latency (median, 5.5 ms; Fig. 5 A , center ). Latencies were similar for units recorded in different regions of the hippocampus (CA1, dentate gyrus, and CA3; median latencies: 6/6.5/5 ms; Kruskal-Wallis test, P = 0.61; Fig. 5 A , inset ). Finally, the temporal precision of light-evoked spiking, quantified by the across-trial standard deviation of the centers-of-mass, was in the millisecond range (median, 2 ms; Fig. 5 A , right ), indicating that weak blue light could yield precise temporal control of concurrently recorded units.
